doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Opportunities for tuba: McCoy Tyner, Carla Bley, Gil Evans, Haden, Blythe
summary: Stewart traces his jobs from Slugs with McCoy Tyner through Carla Bley, Gil Evans, Charlie Haden and Arthur Blythe, and juggling several big band scenes.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Did you find that okay you’re playing an instrument that not as many people play perhaps, especially in the jazz world, so there’s not as much competition on your instrument but there’s not as many opportunities? Or did you make your opportunities?

I think both things are probably true. And to one degree or another both things are true at whatever given time. When I first came to New York the only opportunity for tuba was at Your Father’s Moustache, and soon after that, around ’67, McCoy Tyner had recorded an album called “Tender Moments,” all right? With Lee Morgan and James Spaulding, and just some great players. And he was doing some work with that album in New York at Slugs, it was before McCoy was of the stature to be able to go into the Vanguard and stuff, so we were doing it at Slugs over on the lower east side. And sometimes Howard Johnson, Howard Johnson was on the album on tuba and on baritone sax, he couldn’t make it sometimes so he’d call me and that was my first jazz experience, in McCoy Tyner’s band at the lower east side at Slugs, doing the music from “Tender Moments.” Now that was one of the first jazz opportunities and after that period there weren’t that many. Carla Bley was the next person because JCOA — Jazz Composers Workshop Orchestra — happened. And Carla Bley and Mike Mantler were doing things and they invited me to do tuba on some of their things. I actually sang on one of their — “Escalator Over the Hill,” that, one of those early JCOA albums. And then I played on some of her other things and that’s when I was in her band by the — all that led up to — all that was going on in the beginning of the seventies and by the time we got to around ’76 she took that band out on the road so it was my second experience on the road. My first was with Gil Evans in ’76 and then I went with her later on in the year going to Europe. But those were the two bands at that time that were kind of — so they were performing all the time so every once in a while down at the Loeb Student Center in New York where they gave their concerts — but that building’s been torn down now — they would give concerts. By the mid, late seventies by ’78, ’79, I was doing something with Charlie Haden so it was growing by the end of the seventies. So you’ve got Carla Bley’s band that’s got a tuba book, you’ve got Gil Evans’ band that’s got a tuba book and you’ve got Charlie Haden’s Liberation Orchestra that’s got a tuba book by the beginning of the eighties, and also by the beginning of the eighties I started doing some things with Arthur Blythe, small ensemble things. So I started to mix being a tuba bass player along

with being an ensemble horn player in these big band settings. So there were two different positions that I got a chance to be in. And also because of the many hats that I’ve worn I was playing free jazz in Sam Rivers’ Big Band that was performing and working and rehearsing at this time all through the seventies, I was playing Collective Black Artists Big Winds, which was a kind of a cultural, very ethnic — it was swing and everything but it still had a more cultural and ethnic quality to it. Then I was also working in Frank Foster’s big band which was more straight ahead, Basiesque, you know.

Exactly that. And so I mean I was doing a bunch of these big bands and all of this was in different music. Every band I went in had different musicians. So every one of these bands had a little clique of musicians that were working the bands. So I was going between about three or four different cliques in New York, so I knew a whole bevy of musicians, all of which played different from each other. So I got a chance to see sides of New York that many trumpet players never got a chance to see because they would be in this clique but they wouldn’t be hired for these other three. So I mean this was one of the interesting things and the positives of having those hats. And so I got a chance to see a lot of different music and I brought all of that, and see a lot of different bass players. With Collective Black Artists there was Reggie Workman, there was Buster Williams, and then with Frank Foster there was Earl May, and he’s a very different player than either one of the first two I mentioned. And with Carla Bley there was Steve Swallow, you know what I mean? So I’m like around all these great bass players and so I’m drawing from different colors from them and how to present the bass line and therefore influencing how I try and do it on tuba.
